topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on employer perspectives on AI literacy needs, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the title and snippet provided. Findings may reflect specific industry sectors or regions where surveyed employers operate.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps in your workforce by consulting employers in your sector about which skills matter most — this study captures what employers prioritise, helping you align training to genuine market needs rather than generic AI awareness.

Use employer feedback on curriculum priorities to shape internal upskilling programs — focus on technical capabilities and competencies that employers actively value, rather than theoretical AI knowledge alone.

Bridge readiness gaps through targeted intervention — understand where your workforce currently stands on AI capabilities and design curricula that close gaps between current competency and employer expectations.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development contexts; generalisability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without full article.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption can be converted into readiness through structured development programs; identify specific barriers your team faces (fear, skills gaps, relevance concerns) and address them through targeted training rather than top-down mandates.

Institutional AI literacy initiatives should prioritize teaching educators before they teach others — train-the-trainer models in public health contexts may increase cascade adoption and credibility of AI content.

Position AI literacy as directly relevant to public health problems (disease modeling, data analysis, health equity) rather than as a generic skill — contextualizing AI learning to domain-specific applications increases uptake.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development would require adaptation. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework that embeds AI competencies alongside foundational digital skills may be more effective than siloed AI training — consider whether your organisation's AI literacy programme integrates AI into broader digital capability rather than treating it as standalone.

Middle school curriculum integration suggests scaffolded, age-appropriate progression of AI concepts — apply this principle to adult learners by sequencing AI literacy from foundational conceptual understanding (what AI is, how it works) before advancing to practical application and critical evaluation skills.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health context; may have limited applicability to Australian health systems, governance structures, and regulatory frameworks.
takeaways: Identifies core competencies needed for digital public health roles in European settings; review findings on technical, data literacy, and change management skills may inform competency assessment in Australian health organisations, though local regulatory and system differences should be considered.

Provides a structured framework for mapping skill gaps in public health workforces; useful for designing targeted upskilling programmes, though European competency definitions may need adaptation for Australian context and priorities.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to higher vocational education contexts and may not generalise to corporate workplace settings or different educational levels without further validation.
takeaways: A competency ladder framework can structure AI literacy development in stages, allowing learners to progress from foundational to advanced capabilities — consider adopting a similar scaffolded approach when designing AI upskilling programmes for your employees.

Validation of competency pathways requires both theoretical development and empirical testing; if creating internal AI literacy curricula, build in assessment and feedback loops to ensure the pathway actually builds the intended capabilities.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global data but priorities may vary significantly by industry, geography, and organisational maturity. Australian organisations should validate recommendations against local labour market conditions and skill availability.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will face the highest AI disruption risk, then prioritise upskilling cohorts in those areas first rather than attempting organisation-wide reskilling simultaneously.

Develop a skills audit that distinguishes between foundational AI literacy (what all employees need) and role-specific AI capabilities (what certain teams need), to tailor training investments efficiently.

Create clear career pathways showing how employees can transition into AI-adjacent roles, as reskilling is more likely to succeed when people see advancement opportunities rather than viewing it as defensive training.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot determine from title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, and sector not evident. Full article review needed to assess applicability to Australian organisations.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may have paradoxical effects on creativity — while it can enhance some creative processes, it may simultaneously constrain others depending on implementation approach and role type.
When rolling out AI tools, deliberately assess which creative tasks benefit from automation versus which require human novelty and divergent thinking to avoid unintended creativity suppression.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet; findings on paternalistic leadership may be more applicable to Asian organizational contexts where this leadership style is prevalent, and may not transfer directly to Australian workplaces with flatter hierarchies and less hierarchical norms.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customizing or 'crafting' AI systems to fit their specific work needs — this drives more collaborative use of AI rather than resistance or passive adoption.

If your organization operates under or transitions toward paternalistic leadership, leverage the leader's influence to champion AI adoption; conversely, in more egalitarian settings, emphasize peer influence and collaborative design of AI workflows to achieve similar engagement effects.

Create opportunities for employees to actively shape how AI is implemented in their role (e.g., choosing which AI features to use, suggesting process improvements) — this sense of ownership is a stronger predictor of effective human-AI collaboration than top-down mandates alone.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and geographic scope, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The dual-pathway model may apply broadly to organisations undergoing AI-enabled transformation, but limitations regarding sector, country, and sample size cannot be assessed from available information.
takeaways: AI-enabled workforce transformation creates two distinct psychological pathways: one enhancing capability and empowerment, another triggering anxiety and job insecurity—organisations should design interventions targeting both pathways simultaneously rather than assuming AI upskilling alone resolves employee concerns.

Monitor employee anxiety and job insecurity as distinct outcomes during AI implementation; capability development and empowerment may not automatically reduce these concerns, requiring separate communication and support strategies.
Align AI transformation initiatives with corporate sustainability goals to frame capability development as mutual benefit, potentially shifting employee perception from threat to opportunity.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone. The full article would need to be reviewed to determine sample size, geographic scope, industry focus, and methodology.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviors may diverge when AI is introduced—some employees actively reshape their roles to work alongside AI (approach), while others withdraw or resist engagement (avoidance). Understanding which employees tend toward each response helps tailor adoption support.

An approach-avoidance framework suggests that perceived threat versus opportunity from AI implementation drives employee behavior change. Addressing psychological safety and reframing AI as a tool for skill enhancement rather than replacement may shift more employees toward constructive job crafting.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by unknown sample characteristics — article title and snippet do not indicate geographic scope, sector, sample size, or methodology details. Findings may not transfer across different organisational cultures or AI implementation contexts.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee wellbeing when psychological safety is not actively cultivated — assess your team's sense of safety to voice concerns about AI tools before and during rollout.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions — leaders must transparently communicate AI decision-making processes and demonstrate commitment to human values, not just efficiency gains, to mitigate depression and disengagement risk.

Monitor mental health outcomes alongside adoption metrics — combine depression/wellbeing screening with adoption surveys to catch psychological safety erosion early and adjust implementation approaches.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample characteristics, organisational sectors studied, and whether findings hold across different AI implementation contexts.
takeaways: Design AI collaboration systems that activate both competence (mastery of AI tools) and autonomy (meaningful choice in how employees use AI) to maximise engagement — these dual pathways appear more effective than focusing on either alone.

When introducing AI, explicitly communicate how it expands employee capability and decision-making authority, not just efficiency gains — framing affects which psychological pathways are activated and subsequent engagement levels.

Measure engagement through the lens of these psychological mechanisms (competence and autonomy) rather than just task completion metrics, to identify whether your AI implementation is genuinely transforming how employees experience their work.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective based on consulting experience, but lacks specific empirical data on sample composition, geographic scope, or sector breakdown. Findings likely generalizable to large organizations with resources for structured change programs, but applicability to smaller organizations or specific Australian contexts unclear.
takeaways: Shift focus from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behavioural integration) — this reframing helps teams understand that technical rollout is only the first step; lasting change requires deliberate attention to how people work differently with AI.

Design change programs that explicitly target human behaviors needed for AI success (e.g., comfort with ambiguity, collaborative learning, experimentation mindset) rather than assuming employees will naturally adapt once tools are available.

Use a structured change approach that builds capability progressively — avoid 'train and deploy' models in favor of ongoing behavioral coaching, peer learning, and feedback loops that allow teams to adjust their practices as they integrate AI into real work.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents Stanford GSB perspective on AI and work trends, but lacks empirical data or specific sample information. Insights may reflect US business school viewpoint and may not account for Australian workplace contexts, regulations, or labour market conditions.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI displacement and proactively design upskilling programs for affected employees before disruption occurs.
Create clear communication strategies about how AI will augment (rather than replace) specific roles — ambiguity about AI's impact is a key driver of workplace anxiety and resistance to adoption.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case examples and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Segment your AI transformation into three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, and impact) to avoid treating implementation as a single step and clarify what success looks like at each stage.

Use the 'three horizons' framework to help teams distinguish between early pilots, enterprise-wide rollout, and sustained value creation — this helps manage expectations and resource allocation across different transformation timelines.

Identify and address the behavioural and organisational barriers unique to each horizon (e.g., skill gaps in horizon 1, change resistance in horizon 2, cultural lock-in in horizon 3) rather than applying one-size-fits-all change strategies.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, the geographic scope and sample composition cannot be determined. Findings may be specific to particular organisational contexts or industries.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger two opposing employee responses: some will proactively reshape their roles to leverage AI (approach), while others may withdraw or minimise AI engagement (avoidance) — managers should identify and support both groups differently.

Job crafting interventions during AI rollout could help redirect avoidance responses toward productive adaptation; consider coaching or peer-mentoring programmes that reframe AI as a tool for task redesign rather than threat.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on client work across sectors, but specific case details and applicability to smaller Australian organisations or non-client contexts not specified.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation — this reframing helps prioritise reskilling and role redesign alongside system rollout.
Identify which job functions will change versus disappear, then design targeted transition pathways and upskilling programs before deployment to retain engagement and reduce resistance.
Establish clear communication about how AI will augment (not replace) roles; transparency about future job security and evolution is critical to sustaining employee buy-in during transformation.

articles.title: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a discourse analysis of digital commentary rather than an empirical study, so findings reflect online narratives about AI anxiety rather than measured employee experiences. Generalisability depends on which digital platforms were analysed.
takeaways: Recognise that employee anxiety about AI is often rooted in perceived threats to the psychological contract (job security, autonomy, fairness) rather than AI capability alone — address these underlying concerns explicitly in change communications.

Monitor and engage with employee discourse about AI across internal communication channels to identify specific anxieties early, allowing you to co-design AI implementation approaches that rebuild trust in the psychological contract.

Frame AI adoption conversations around what the psychological contract will look like after implementation — clarity on roles, value, and job security is more likely to reduce anxiety than technical reassurance alone.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research on social connection and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific findings may vary by cultural context.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable effects on physical health outcomes — people with close social ties have lower rates of heart disease, stroke, and mortality compared to isolated individuals.

The health benefits of friendship work through both direct physiological pathways (reduced stress hormones, stronger immune function) and indirect behavioural ones (friends encourage healthier habits and provide emotional support during hardship).
Quality matters more than quantity — a few meaningful, reciprocal friendships protect health more effectively than a large network of shallow connections.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Low — headline claim lacks supporting detail. Actual scope, sample size, and methodology unknown from snippet alone.
takeaways: Genetics may account for a larger share of personality variation than previously thought — challenging the nature-vs-nurture consensus and suggesting our traits are stickier than we assume.
If true, this finding is counterintuitive because it runs against decades of psychological emphasis on environmental and situational factors shaping who we are.
The result matters to anyone curious about identity: it hints that efforts to 'reinvent' ourselves may face biological headwinds, though genes are rarely destiny.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — suggests cross-cultural patterns in music-personality links, though specific cultural contexts and music genres studied would affect applicability.
takeaways: People's taste in music reveals consistent personality patterns regardless of where they live — your playlist might say more about your temperament than your passport.
This challenges the idea that culture completely shapes musical preference, hinting at universal psychological patterns underlying what we enjoy listening to.
A surprising counterintuitive angle: even though music is deeply tied to culture and identity, the fundamental personality signals it sends appear remarkably consistent across the globe.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises psychological research on true crime fascination, but specific study populations and geographic contexts of underlying research not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: People aren't morbidly weird for binge-watching true crime — psychologists have identified legitimate cognitive and emotional reasons we're drawn to dark stories, from threat detection to narrative puzzle-solving.
True crime consumption might scratch an itch for understanding human evil and injustice in a controlled, safe way — letting us explore the darker corners of human behaviour without real danger.
The 'true crime boom' reveals something unexpected: our fascination isn't new, but technology and streaming platforms have simply made these stories infinitely more accessible than ever before.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesizes existing research on MBTI validity, but findings depend on quality and scope of studies reviewed; limited to English-language literature.
takeaways: Despite its massive popularity in corporate settings, the MBTI has surprisingly weak empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviors — the gap between how widely it's used and what the science shows is striking.

The 'type' framework may be too rigid: people don't neatly fit into boxes, and behavior varies dramatically by context, making fixed personality categories unreliable predictors of how someone will actually lead.

The finding highlights a fascinating pattern in organizational psychology — tools become culturally entrenched (MBTI is everywhere) regardless of whether the evidence backs them up, revealing how organizations crave simple answers to complex human questions.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a general-audience commentary piece rather than empirical research, so findings reflect expert interpretation rather than systematic evidence.
takeaways: Dogs likely process social cues and emotions differently than humans, which helps explain why they're so attuned to our moods even when we're not consciously signalling.
Understanding canine cognition challenges human-centric assumptions about intelligence and learning, revealing that 'thinking' looks radically different across species.
The gap between what dogs actually think and what we assume they're thinking is surprisingly wide — a humbling reminder that animal minds operate on their own logic, not ours.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample source and geography not indicated in snippet. Findings may not generalise across different organisational contexts, cultures, or AI implementation approaches without additional methodological detail.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent attention to psychological safety and ethical leadership can increase employee depression; assess your team's psychological safety before and during AI rollout, not after.

Ethical leadership is a buffer against negative mental health outcomes during AI transitions — explicitly model transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledge uncertainty, and involve employees in setting AI governance boundaries.

Monitor psychological safety indicators (voice, risk-taking, interpersonal trust) as leading indicators of employee wellbeing during AI adoption, rather than waiting for depression or burnout to emerge.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may reflect practices and contexts most relevant to large enterprises and developed economies. Applicability to smaller organisations or different cultural contexts not specified.
takeaways: Design AI implementations to enhance employee agency and decision-making autonomy rather than replace human judgment — 'superagency' requires clear role clarity about when and how people oversee, redirect, or veto AI recommendations.

Establish psychological safety practices that explicitly address AI uncertainty: create channels for employees to flag AI errors without penalty, normalise healthy scepticism of AI outputs, and ensure accountability structures protect people who question algorithmic decisions.

articles.title: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet. Without knowing the geographic scope, sector, sample size, or methodology, it is difficult to assess how broadly findings about AI anxiety and deviant innovation apply across different organisational contexts.
takeaways: Monitor and address AI-related anxiety in your team, as it may drive employees toward unauthorised workarounds or shortcuts rather than sanctioned processes — creating both risk and innovation opportunities that need careful management.

Consider how your organisational context (leadership style, psychological safety climate, resources) either amplifies or buffers employee anxiety about AI — tailored interventions may be more effective than one-size-fits-all AI upskilling.

Create legitimate channels for employees to propose alternative AI approaches or voice concerns about mandated tools; this may reduce hidden deviant behaviour and surface valuable insights about implementation gaps.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific evidence base and sample composition are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Psychological safety acts as an equaliser in organisations, helping employees from underrepresented or marginalised groups feel more confident contributing ideas and speaking up — consider how your team's norms and leader behaviours either reinforce or diminish this effect.

Creating level playing fields requires intentional structural and cultural interventions beyond individual manager training — audit where psychological safety gaps exist (e.g. by demographic group, tenure, or function) and design targeted responses.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings — while psychological safety principles are universal, this report reflects American workplace contexts, labour practices, and demographic composition that may not directly transfer to Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Identify specific psychological safety gaps in your team by assessing whether employees feel safe speaking up about mistakes, disagreements, and new ideas — use this as a diagnostic baseline before designing interventions.
Link psychological safety outcomes to measurable business metrics (retention, innovation, wellbeing) to build stakeholder buy-in for safety-focused culture changes in your organisation.

Recognise that psychological safety needs may differ across demographic groups and roles — avoid one-size-fits-all approaches; tailor safety initiatives based on how different employee cohorts experience trust and belonging.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on Harvard expertise but lacks empirical data or geographic specificity. Applies broadly to organisational contexts, though examples may be US-centric given the institutional source.
takeaways: Clarify what psychological safety actually means in your team — it's not about being 'nice' or avoiding accountability, but about trust to speak up without fear of embarrassment or punishment.
Address common myths (e.g., that PS eliminates conflict or lowers performance standards) when communicating the concept to leaders, as misconceptions often derail implementation efforts.
Use this framing to counter resistance: psychological safety improves decision-making and error detection by enabling candid feedback, not by lowering expectations.
